messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Gerald is a 66-year-old married software engineer of European descent who presented for psychological assessment reporting a cluster of distressing symptoms that, on careful inquiry, traced their roots to a childhood marked by repeated physical abuse at the hands of a primary caregiver. He described years of unpredictable violence — being grabbed without warning, struck with open hands or household objects, and held down in ways that left him acutely sensitised to the physical world around him. Cold air against his skin in winter, the particular chill of an air-conditioned room, the sudden warmth of a hand reaching toward him — these were the textures of danger in his earliest years, and they have never fully lost that meaning.

Gerald spent decades constructing a life that kept those memories at arm's length. A career in software engineering suited him: solitary, logical, mediated through screens rather than bodies. For many years the strategy worked tolerably well. But in his early sixties, a minor cardiac event left him hyperaware of his own physiology, and it was as though a door he had kept shut for forty years swung open. When his heart pounds now — during a brisk walk, after a second cup of coffee, in a moment of mild exertion — the sensation arrives not as a neutral fact but as an alarm. The racing pulse pulls a sudden, unbidden memory forward: the specific weight of fear in his chest as a child, the sense of the body bracing before the mind has caught up. That intrusive memory, arriving whole and without context, immediately sharpens his perception of the environment around him. He finds himself scanning his home office for objects that could serve as weapons — a heavy stapler, a letter opener, the corner of a monitor stand — and his body has already tensed before he has consciously registered why. The link between the somatic trigger and the threat response is nearly instantaneous, as though his nervous system has never updated its threat model from childhood.

What has hardened over time is not merely the fear itself but the conclusions Gerald has drawn from it. He has come to believe, with quiet certainty, that people cannot be trusted — that warmth is a prelude to harm, that closeness is a form of exposure. He experiences himself as permanently set apart: a man who can function among others but never truly belong to them. These convictions feel to him not like symptoms but like hard-won realism, the sensible conclusions of a man who paid attention. And it is precisely because he holds them as truths that they govern his behaviour so completely. He avoids physical contact with near-totality — he has not embraced his wife spontaneously in longer than either of them can comfortably name. He has gradually withdrawn from the small circle of colleagues and neighbours he once socialised with, finding reasons not to attend gatherings, not to answer invitations. He will not look at or attend to his own body beyond what hygiene requires, as though the body itself is a site too dangerous to examine.

These strategies, which feel to Gerald like prudent self-protection, have in practice tightened the very conditions they were meant to relieve. His social withdrawal has confirmed, in his experience, that he is an outsider — because he is now, functionally, outside. His avoidance of touch has made any accidental contact — a colleague brushing past him in a hallway, his wife's hand on his shoulder — land with startling force, his whole system reacting with alarm before he has time to think. The avoidance keeps the threat system primed and the appraisals unchallenged, so that a cool breeze through an open window or a sudden flutter in his chest is enough to reinstate the full vigilance of a frightened child. His negative beliefs about the world, never tested against disconfirming experience, continue to generate the hypervigilance that makes every temperature change and every heartbeat feel like a signal worth attending to.

What finally brought Gerald to seek help was his wife's quiet statement, delivered without accusation, that she felt she had lost him. He came to the first session uncertain whether he could be helped and more uncertain still whether he deserved to be — but beneath that, something that might cautiously be called hope.
